items.title: [npr.org] Alaska Native villages remain displaced a year after Typhoon Halong
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

Kwigillingok damage: The storm surge rose more than 6.3 feet above the normal highest-tide line and swept 46 of Kwigillingok’s 99 houses off their foundations (insideclimatenews.org). Work stoppage: Kwigillingok had no construction crews on the ground from early September to mid-October as crews waited for Federal Emergency Management Agency funding (insideclimatenews.org). Kipnuk homes: Alaska’s Emergency Operations Center estimated 90% of Kipnuk residences were damaged; the town has fewer than 200 homes and is consistently accessible mainly by plane (npr.org).

items.title: [cbc.ca] Blackstone-led group to invest in Mitsubishi’s LNG Canada stake
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A Blackstone-led group that includes four Canadian pension funds agreed to invest US$3.1 billion for a 49.9% interest in a Mitsubishi Corp. subsidiary that holds Mitsubishi’s 15% stake in LNG Canada, the export terminal near Kitimat, British Columbia. The investors will hold an indirect interest in the project, not a direct 49.9% share of LNG Canada. Mitsubishi says the sale will improve capital efficiency and help finance LNG Canada’s Phase 2 expansion, which the project’s partners approved on Sept. 29. The expansion is expected to double capacity to 28 million tonnes a year; Mitsubishi will retain its existing LNG supply rights. Environmental and Indigenous advocates criticized the pension funds’ participation, citing climate risks and objections to the project. The transaction is expected to close in November.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

This huge and impressive Bronze Age tomb is about 5 minutes walk from the SP 38 road. 

There are directional arrows on the ground, consisting of stones arranged into arrow shapes, each of which is unique.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] Google bans Chinese partner after backdoor infects 1.3 million Android boxes
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Google and security partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes. Google says it has high confidence that Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately embedded the backdoor in device firmware and sold criminal groups access to infected hardware. The criminal groups used the devices to commit advertising fraud, route other people’s internet traffic through household connections and install additional malware. Google also reported that operators captured screens, collected account information and system logs, and issued commands remotely. The same malware appeared on telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signs. Google’s takedown targeted XCPE control servers and domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Google estimates the takedown could also cut criminal access to at least 10 million other devices compromised through separate routes. Videostrong evaded Google’s device checks by loading malicious code after a device’s first boot, Google said. Google has banned Videostrong and its future affiliates from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers, and says it changed its review process. The backdoor remains in affected devices and can reinstall after a reboot. Synthient, a security firm involved in the investigation, recommends disconnecting and replacing affected boxes.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. items.title: [pbs.org] Super El Niño nears December peak as extreme weather spreads
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The exceptionally strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is intensifying weather risks across several regions, including heavy rain and flash floods in the U.S. Southwest. Scientists say the pattern adds moisture to the air and shifts winds, making downpours more likely, although it is not the sole cause of individual storms. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to peak in December and persist into February 2027. The agency says it could rank among the strongest since at least 1950. Flooding has also been reported in Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and parts of Southeast Asia are unusually dry. In the Southwest, flooding prompted evacuations, and the San Juan River threatened Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Warmer oceans linked to human-caused climate change may amplify the event’s effects, but scientists caution that separating El Niño’s contribution from the long-term warming trend remains difficult. In September, sea-surface temperature in the Pacific’s Niño 3.4 reference region reached 29.70°C, while the global ocean average for that month, excluding polar waters, set a September record of 21.05°C. Forecasters expect the strongest effects to continue into 2027.
